{{Short description|Extension of ideas in combinatorics to infinite sets}}

{{inline citations|date=May 2024}}
In mathematics, '''infinitary combinatorics''', or '''combinatorial set theory''', is an extension of ideas in [[combinatorics]] to [[infinite set]]s.
Some of the things studied include [[continuous graph]]s and [[tree (set theory)|trees]], extensions of [[Ramsey's theorem]], and [[Martin's axiom]].
Recent developments concern combinatorics of the [[continuum (set theory)|continuum]]<ref>[[Andreas Blass]], ''Combinatorial Cardinal Characteristics of the Continuum'', Chapter 6 in Handbook of Set Theory, edited by [[Matthew Foreman]] and [[Akihiro Kanamori]], Springer, 2010</ref> and combinatorics on successors of singular cardinals.<ref>Todd Eisworth, ''Successors of Singular Cardinals'' Chapter 15 in Handbook of Set Theory, edited by Matthew Foreman and Akihiro Kanamori, Springer, 2010</ref>

==Ramsey theory for infinite sets==
Write <math>\kappa, \lambda</math> for ordinals,  <math>m</math> for a [[cardinal number]] (finite or infinite) and <math>n</math> for a natural number. {{harvtxt|Erdős|Rado|1956}} introduced the notation
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\kappa\rightarrow(\lambda)^n_m</math>}}
as a shorthand way of saying that every [[partition of a set|partition]] of the set <math>[\kappa]^n</math> of <math>n</math>-element [[subset]]s of <math>\kappa</math> into <math>m</math> pieces has a homogeneous set of order type <math>\lambda</math>. A homogeneous set is in this case a subset of <math>\kappa</math> such that every <math>n</math>-element subset is in the same element of the partition. When <math>m</math> is 2 it is often omitted. Such statements are known as partition relations.

Assuming the [[axiom of choice]], there are no ordinals <math>\kappa</math> with <math>\kappa\rightarrow(\omega)^{\omega}</math>, so <math>n</math> is usually taken to be finite. An extension where <math>n</math> is almost allowed to be infinite is the notation
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\kappa\rightarrow(\lambda)^{<\omega}_m</math>}}
which is a shorthand way of saying that every [[partition of a set|partition]] of the set of finite subsets of <math>\kappa</math> into <math>m</math> pieces has a subset of order type <math>\lambda</math> such that for any finite <math>n</math>, all subsets of size <math>n</math> are in the same element of the partition. When <math>m</math> is 2 it is often omitted.

Another variation is the notation
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\kappa\rightarrow(\lambda, \mu)^n</math>}}
which is a shorthand way of saying that every coloring of the set <math>[\kappa]^n</math> of <math>n</math>-element subsets of <math>\kappa</math> with 2 colors has a subset  of order type <math>\lambda</math> such that all elements of <math>[\lambda]^n</math> have the first color, or a subset  of order type <math>\mu</math> such that all elements of <math>[\mu]^n</math> have the second color. A coloring of <math>[\kappa]^n</math>is a function <math>f : [\kappa]^n \rightarrow p</math>.

Some properties of this include: (in what follows <math>\kappa</math> is a cardinal)
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\alef_0\rightarrow(\alef_0)^n_k</math> for all finite <math>n</math> and <math>k</math> ([[Ramsey's theorem]]).}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\beth_n^+\rightarrow(\alef_1)_{\alef_0}^{n+1}</math> (the [[Erdős–Rado theorem]].)}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle2^\kappa\not\rightarrow(\kappa^+)^2</math> (the Sierpiński theorem)}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle2^\kappa\not\rightarrow(3)^2_\kappa</math>}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\kappa\rightarrow(\kappa,\alef_0)^2</math> (the [[Erdős–Dushnik–Miller theorem]])}}

In choiceless universes, partition properties with infinite exponents may hold, and some of them are obtained as consequences of the [[axiom of determinacy]] (AD). For example, [[Donald A. Martin]] proved that AD implies  
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\alef_1\rightarrow(\alef_1)^{\alef_1}_2</math>}}

==Strong colorings==
[[Wacław Sierpiński]] showed that the Ramsey theorem does not extend to sets of size <math>\alef_1</math>by showing that <math>2^{\alef_0}\nrightarrow(\alef_1)^2_2</math>. That is, Sierpiński constructed a coloring of pairs of [[real numbers]] into two colors such that for every uncountable subset of real numbers <math>X</math>, <math>[X]^2</math> takes both colors. Taking any set of real numbers of size <math>\alef_1</math> and applying the coloring of Sierpiński to it, we get that <math>\alef_1\not\rightarrow(\alef_1)^2_2</math>. Colorings such as this are known as strong colorings<ref>{{citation |url=https://blog.assafrinot.com/?p=4392 |title=Tutorial on strong colorings and their applications, 6th European Set Theory Conference |first=Assaf |last=Rinot |access-date=2023-12-10}}</ref> and studied in set theory. {{harvtxt|Erdős|Hajnal|Rado|1965}} introduced a similar notation as above for this.

Write <math>\kappa, \lambda</math> for ordinals,  <math>m</math> for a cardinal number (finite or infinite) and <math>n</math> for a natural number. Then
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\kappa\nrightarrow[\lambda]^n_m</math>}}
is a shorthand way of saying that there exists a coloring of the set <math>[\kappa]^n</math> of <math>n</math>-element subsets of <math>\kappa</math> into <math>m</math> pieces such that every set of order type <math>\lambda</math> is a rainbow set. A rainbow set is in this case a subset <math>A</math> of <math>\kappa</math> such that <math>[A]^n</math> takes all <math>m</math> colors. When <math>m</math> is 2 it is often omitted. Such statements are known as negative square bracket partition relations.

Another variation is the notation
:<math>\kappa\nrightarrow[\lambda; \mu]^2_m</math>
which is a shorthand way of saying that there exists a coloring of the set <math>[\kappa]^2</math> of 2-element subsets of <math>\kappa</math> with <math>m</math> colors such that for every subset <math>A</math> of order type <math>\lambda</math> and every subset <math>B</math> of order type <math>\mu</math>, the set <math>A\times B</math> takes all <math>m</math> colors.

Some properties of this include: (in what follows <math>\kappa</math> is a cardinal)
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle2^\kappa\nrightarrow[\kappa^+]^2</math> (Sierpiński)}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\alef_1\nrightarrow[\alef_1]^2</math> (Sierpiński)}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\alef_1\nrightarrow[\alef_1]^2_{3}</math> ([[Richard Laver|Laver]], [[Andreas Blass|Blass]])}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\alef_1\nrightarrow[\alef_1]^2_{4}</math> ([[Fred Galvin| Galvin]] and [[Saharon Shelah|Shelah]])}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\alef_1\nrightarrow[\alef_1]^2_{\alef_1}</math> ([[Stevo Todorčević|Todorčević]])}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle\alef_1\nrightarrow[\alef_1; \alef_1]^2_{\alef_1}</math> ([[Justin T. Moore|Moore]])}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>\displaystyle2^{\alef_0}\nrightarrow[2^{\alef_0}]^2_{\alef_0}</math> ([[Fred Galvin| Galvin]] and [[Saharon Shelah|Shelah]])}}

==Large cardinals==
Several [[large cardinal]] properties can be defined using this notation. In particular:
*[[Weakly compact cardinal]]s <math>\kappa</math> are those that satisfy <math>\kappa\rightarrow(\kappa)^2</math>
*α-[[Erdős cardinal]]s <math>\kappa</math> are the smallest that satisfy <math>\kappa\rightarrow(\alpha)^{<\,\omega}</math>
*[[Ramsey cardinal]]s <math>\kappa</math> are those that satisfy <math>\kappa\rightarrow(\kappa)^{<\,\omega}</math>
